title: Domain Restriction via SAE Multi-Layer Transitions
claim: Layer-wise sparse encodings of internal activations form a depth trajectory that a lightweight sequential scorer uses to flag out-of-domain inputs.
layout: 4 columns, left-to-right, per-layer rows stacked bottom-to-top, curved arrows to states
description: A four-column diagram reads left to right. The first column is a decoder-only transformer drawn as a rounded gray container. It holds stacked rows of token boxes separated by blue 'Attention Block' bars, labeled Layer 1, Layer 2, Layer 3 and Last Layer, with input token boxes entering from the bottom. Each layer has an arrow to a pink SAE encoder/decoder trapezoid pair beside a vertical sparse-code vector of numbers such as 47, 9 and 10. A curved arrow from each SAE leads to a binary TopK vector of 0s and 1s. Arrows labeled first, second and final state feed a tall gray box reading 'HTM / Markov Chain / RNN' (Sequence Scorer). A speech bubble saying ANOMALY sits at its upper right. Column headers are in bold.
caption: Pipeline overview. Given an input, we extract residual-stream activations across layers, encode them with layer-wise SAEs, pool over tokens, mask globally frequent features, and binarize via Top-$k$ to obtain an SAE$\rightarrow$SDR depth trajectory. A lightweight sequential scorer (Markov/HTM/RNN) trained on ID-only data assigns an anomaly score from depthwise transitions.
abstract: The general-purpose nature of Large Language Models (LLMs) presents a significant challenge for domain-specific applications, often leading to out-of-domain (OOD) interactions that undermine the provider's intent. Existing methods for detecting such scenarios treat the LLM as an uninterpretable black box and overlook the internal processing of inputs. In this work we show that layer transitions provide a promising avenue for extracting domain-specific signature. Specifically, we present several lightweight ways of learning on internal dynamics encoded using a sparse autoencoder (SAE) that exhibit great capability in distinguishing OOD texts. Building on top of SAEs representation transitions enables us to better interpret the LLM internal evolution of input processing and shed light on its decisions. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the method and benchmark it with the gemma-2 2B and 9B models. Our results emphasize the efficacy of the internal process in capturing fine-grained input-related details.
